utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, do you feel well enough to continue after the dentist of this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the trial to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one additional question related to the topic we were discussing yesterday, if I could ask you to turn to two tabs in the binder we were using yesterday. First is tab 201. 201 contains excerpts from the 34th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in 1993. That's P64, P65, tab 221.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the Court could turn to page 64 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We brought some material but not 201.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I mean, I do have it but it wasn't in the tab. That's why we are getting an insert, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it in front of us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As indicated Mr. Krajisnik, it was the bottom of page 64 in the English and in the B/C/S page 62. These are remarks by Dr. Karadzic. It's also at the bottom of your page, Mr. Krajisnik, ending with the ERN number 0570.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm beginning with the -- it's approximately six lines up from the bottom. Dr. Karadzic states, "Personally I think that we gain more. Sarajevo is not in the Muslim state," and again let me pause and say this is in the context of discussions clearly about yet another plan. And again Dr. Karadzic states, "Personally I think that we gain more. Sarajevo is not in the Muslim state. It is in a Serbian state because everything around is Serbian and we keep everything. We are not going to cede a single footstep. If we would cede a single footstep on their pressure we will finish the job. Therefore, Sarajevo has more chances to become entirely Serbian than to become entirely Muslim. The most probable option is to divide Sarajevo and create two cities. We will not cede Sarajevo, gentlemen. We frankly said that to delegations." And if you could then turn quickly to tab 191, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you skipping lines? You start reading and then you skip a line or lines, and then I cannot follow what you're saying. Yes, because the interpreter was saying "Sarajevo is not," et cetera, and I can't find that so I can't follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krajisnik, I am not skipping lines in so far as I am aware, but reading directly from the translation at the noted pages.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then the interpreter does not have the original and that is why I cannot follow. Now, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did your version begin with, "Personally I" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you find it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally think that we get more -- I heard you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And then if I ask you to move to tab 191, which contains --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P850, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- which contains an interview with you in Srpska Oslobodjenje, and if I could ask you, Mr. Krajisnik, to turn to -- well, Your Honours, to turn to page 10 of the English, the last passage, and Mr. Krajisnik, for you, that would be the end of the interview, the last full paragraph at the bottom right portion of the article on page 03597315. It's the page that shows you sitting at your desk with a book open in front of you, and the telephone to your left. I can see you're looking at it there. Okay. That part begins by the prospective for Sarajevo is such that in the future, it will not be the capital. God willing, Belgrade will be the capital of all Serb lands, Sarajevo will be our capital until all Serb lands unite. And then I just wanted to continue a few sentences to where you say, "This --" this is now on page 11, Your Honours, the last paragraph. "This is where it's being proven that we cannot talk about some joint country." And that was beginning at the second line in the English on page 11. "We are talking about two towns," you said "two countries here. That is the first phase. I will say, tell you now publicly what I think for the first time to the Oslobodjenje. The prospective for Sarajevo is such that in the future, it will be a unified town but a Serb one completely. The Muslims will have to look nor a capital outside of Sarajevo, somewhere else. That is the natural course of things." Mr. Krajisnik, these two passages in -- at the 34th Assembly by Dr. Karadzic and in Srpska Oslobodjenje by you, reflect the Bosnian Serb leadership's intention that if Sarajevo was to be -- belong to Muslims and Serbs both, it would be two cities and divided and if it was to be one city only, it would be Serb. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not right, Mr. Prosecutor. Please take the plan from this period of time and you will see the international negotiators proposed that two-thirds belonged to the Muslims and one-third to the Serbs, of the inner city that is. And find that plan and you will see that's the way it is. I have no idea what this is here, the way it was put here, but that is what the contact group plan was at the time. And what was proposed then was the possibility of a confederation between us and Serbia. You're taking this out of context. You see what it says here, "there is no bargaining regarding our Sarajevo." I can reed it out. And you will see that it's not what you've been saying. "Today, I presented Mr. Karadzic's statement of the 19th of March." Please, have a look at that and then you will see about what was discussed yesterday, what was claimed yesterday, what is true is what he actually stated, not that there would be a Berlin Wall. Please, let me read out what I said here. Let me read it out and you will see what I said. "We could have had a confederal link with Serbia on the basis of the contact plan. However, we did not accept that plan." I kindly ask that I be allowed to read it so that you will see what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if there is a portion of the article that you think the Judges -- that should be brought to the Court's attention, by all means, point it out, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out now. "Now we hold perhaps 20 per cent of Sarajevo. We are entitled to another 30 per cent of the town. The inner part of the city is" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik please slow down? The interpreters have not found this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you please slow down until the interpreters have found the relevant passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm going to repeat what I read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "We are now holding perhaps 20 per cent of Sarajevo. We are entitled to another 30 per cent of the town. The municipality of Stari Grad, centre of Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad, belong to the inner part of the city. In that Novo Sarajevo, New Sarajevo, we hold only Grbavica. We have a right to half of this inner urban area. All the rest is the periphery. By no means can we cede parts of Sarajevo that are held by the Serbs. We can only talk about possible exchanges." And so on and so forth. That was the plan of the contact group that was supposed to give the entire urban area to the Muslims. Please, the context is very important, the period of time when this is actually being stated. I brought here today four solutions for Sarajevo. Please, in all four the international community proposed divisions of Sarajevo. We never proposed that. We asked for a district. So I brought all these documents in today and I would like to hand them over to you. I know what we were asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The material you brought today, Mr. Krajisnik, is, as usual, made available to the parties or will be made available to the parties. Since you are drawing our attention to the element of time, the part read to you by Mr. Tieger is followed by a passage which reads, "This town will belong to the Republika Srpska in its totality. All this that I'm saying might seem too optimistic or too radical to you but I'm certain that it will be so. As far as the transitional period is concerned, there will be two towns. It is our goal to achieve all this without war, but I doubt that the Muslims want the same. I'm afraid that for this reason, the deciding battle of this war will take place exactly here, in Sarajevo." In the interview, Mr. Krajisnik, it is reflected that you would have said that it would be not immediately but a longer-term goal to make the whole of Sarajevo belong to the Republika Srpska. Were your words misrepresented here or is it that it was only temporarily that you opted for a -- for two towns rather than one or a divided town or whatever name you gave it? Or if your words are misrepresented, then of course we don't have to pay further attention to it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to be able to read this interview. I don't know. I cannot relate this to what I wrote earlier on. What is referred to here is the capital, because there was a problem between Banja Luka and Sarajevo. Allow me to read this and then I'll see. I never asked for all of Sarajevo to be Serb. No way is that possible. So what are we asking for? Half of the city?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I only say that this is what the publication in -- says which was just read to you by Mr. Tieger, but if you say, "I never said such a thing," then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish I could read the interview. Then I can say why I stated something, if I stated it at all. I don't want to speak just off the cuff as to whether I stated something or not, or why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps, Mr. Krajisnik, you read the last portion of what was -- was it 201 or -- no, it was not 201.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was 191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 191. Could Mr. Krajisnik be given an opportunity to read also the lines that follow the lines quoted by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, that's what it says here, a confederacy. That's what it says here. I know that. Some people say that we will have -- or some people complained that we will have a confederation with Serbia. That wasn't the contact plan. And now I am saying something here, perhaps in a resigned manner, I don't know what I was saying. But any way, I stand by every interview I gave. I just wanted to be in its integral form and I want to be able to read it. I never said things that I did not mean. I did not say them if I meant something else. This is about the plan of the contacts group where they are talking about Sarajevo. I don't know. I cannot say now, just off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had an opportunity to read the last portion of your Oslobodjenje interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand the witness to be saying he wants to read the whole of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then he'll be -- can take that out. Of course, I have drawn his attention to the portion following the lines read by -- read by Mr. Tieger but Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps you -- if there are other parts you'd like to read, they do not all seem to be related exactly to this issue but then you'll have an opportunity to take them with you during the next break and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I stand by every interview I gave. I want to read the interview and I want to see why this was stated and in what context, and I'm never going to deny if I said something, if I said something wrong, too. But if it's the contact group, I know why it was there. And not have someone now come up with some quotation and then ask me to answer. This is not my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I said you will have an opportunity to read 191 and then give further comment on the matter. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The additional bundles is -- could the next couple of additional bundles be distributed, if they are not already available. I know they look daunting. I hope they won't prove be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please verify that Mr. Krajisnik has tab 191 available to him in the original language. That is not new bundle but the old one. That's the Oslobodjenje interview. Yes, if it's there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, during the course of your examination-in-chief, you were asked about the 24 April 1992 decision by the National Security Council stating that the exchange of prisoners be handled by the Ministry of Justice after the internal affairs organs finish their work. And you indicated in your testimony, at -- on May 15th, 2006, at approximately 10.07 through 10.09 that that was the first time that this problem was dealt with in minutes and records and later on several occasions that was an item on the agenda. I'd like to look both at some of the subsequent documentation and some of those items on the agenda. Very quickly, if we can, that just for your benefit and the Court, the April 24th meeting of the Council for National Security and Government is found at tab 253. I've already referred to that. If we could turn quickly to tab 255, P436, that was --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was the decision to form a central commission for the exchange of prisoners of war, arrested persons and the bodies of those killed on May 8th, 1992. And quickly turning also to tab 267 which is P435, P583, tab 75 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me get this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I may be moving fast. I don't mean to rush you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, but you are rushing, but never mind, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You tell me if I'm moving too fast, Mr. Krajisnik and if you need time to find the appropriate passage.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead. I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 267 contains P435, P583 tab 75, and that's an order on June 6, 1992, by the president of the central commission for exchange of prisoners of war, detainees and bodies of the killed, which the Court and the parties have had an opportunity to look at before and in fact was discussed more than once during the course of the case thus far. I wanted you to look at those quickly, Mr. Krajisnik, because those documents reflect the subsequent actions in connection with the exchange of prisoners that took place after the 24 April 1992 decision by the NSC, correct? That is, that after the April 24th decision, a commission was formed for the exchange and that commission went into operation and issued the order we've seen on June 6th.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was first a conference where it was agreed to conduct an all-for-all exchange. And that was -- that gave rise to talks at this consultative meeting. The government was supposed to implement it. And all this explanation that I was unaware of was given us in the testimony of Mr. Mandic. And there is a contract that I have produced, signed by Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Vanovac, from the Serb side, whereas the Muslim side rejected it. There is another contract signed by Mr. Vanovac and Mr. Filip Vukovic but it was never implemented and Mandic gave evidence as to why it wasn't. But I don't know anything about that. I just heard it here, same as you did. I provided that contract among other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during the course of your examination-in-chief, while discussing the decision of the April 24th -- the decision at the April 24th, 1992, NSC session, you mentioned essentially the same thing or alluded to the same thing, when you said, "The Serb side and through the mediation of the UN, that all prisoners at that point in time should be exchanged all for all." Then you indicated that was not realised. You said you didn't know why. And stated that this was simply a big mistake and many remained in prison and then they were easy prey for many irresponsible people in terms of abuse and how should I put this, grave consequences. So that's -- so what you said a moment ago was another reference to the problems arising from the -- the problems that you considered that arose from the problem to implement the all-for-all agreement or to implement exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We always wanted to complete this and have the prisoners exchanged. There were prisoners from the very start, if you remember, and every corps had its own commission for prisoner exchanges, apart from the central commission, meaning prisoners of war that they took prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the order of June 6, 1992, found at tab 267 begins by stating central commission of Serbian Republic of BH for exchange of prisoners of war, detainees and then bodies of the killed. So it distinguishes between prisoner of war and detainees. That distinction, Mr. Krajisnik, is essentially the distinction between prisoners of war and civilian prisoners, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. You're asking me about something that you're reading from that paper. I don't know anything about this. You had Mr. Mandic here and you could have asked him. Indeed, you did ask him. I have no idea about this. I see it here just as you do. I can only guess what the author meant. Those can be prisoners guilty of theft or I don't know. Not necessarily civilian population. Maybe it was a soldier who committed a violation, a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to tab 254, P529, tab 167 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Tieger, the document also is talking about children and minors up to 16 years of age.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't even read the order to the end because I have nothing to do with it. I only saw it here when Mr. Mandic testified. Of course, this seems to be a warning to the government, written by Tolovic. That's how I understand it. Whether such things happened or not can only be explained by the people who did it. I had never seen this order before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had directed your attention, Mr. Krajisnik, and the Court's attention to tab 254. That's a letter by the president of the government or the Prime Minister, to the TO headquarters and to the Serbian MUP on April 28th, 1992, and if we look at the third item --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but this is completely illegible, the copy that I have. It's legible in English, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger would you please read the passage you want to draw the attention of Mr. Krajisnik to, and I don't remember but there must have been a better copy once.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour, and I believe we have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I could not imagine someone would translate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, at the third item which you now have before you in B/C/S, states, in the treatment of prisoners concerning their accommodation, food and medical care --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, the interpreters are very sorry to interrupt but for this to be interpreted as it is written the interpreters need a copy, one copy at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see you have an opportunity to look at it but I presume the Court wants me to read it out and if that's going to be done, the interpreters will need the correct B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We've got it now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be a different copy of -- well, must be the same text but the one bears stamps which the other seems not to bear, different ERN number so it's not just a matter of availability, but also --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that that's right, Your Honour,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Krajisnik, item 3 states, "in the treatment of prisoners concerning their accommodation, food, and medical care, internationally established standards must be observed. A record should be maintained and regularly updated with information on the status of health of both military and civilian prisoners. So that document reflects the distinction between prisoners of war and civilian prisoners that appears to be also reflected in the June 6th order of Mr. Colovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were in prisons both military and civilian prisoners. I mean captured soldiers and civilian persons. Whether he meant by this that they had captured civilian persons, I don't know. But it says detained military and civilian persons. They must have known in prison who was a captured soldier and who was a civilian. Civilians could also be placed under arrest for, I don't know what for, but both categories were in prison. It doesn't mean that a civilian was captured during fighting. I'm talking about things I don't know. I'm just trying to assist. I don't believe that Mr. Djeric would have accepted arrests of civilians. He just believes that there are military prisoners and civilian prisoners in prisons. I mean, civilians who are in prison. I don't know, but from what I know of the man, he would have never accepted for civilians to be arrested and placed in prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, let's look, then, at some of the documents reflecting how persons ended up in camps and ended up in camps for exchange. If we could look at tab 261, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P865, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's an order dated 28 May 1992, by Major Svetozar Andric, the commander of the Birac Brigade, and if we look at item number 6, it states, "The moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and coordinated with the municipalities through which the moving is carried out. Only women and children can move out while men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange." And in connection with that document, Mr. Krajisnik, if we can look quickly also at tab 264, that's P668, Your Honours, that is an order by Major Andric dated 31 May 1992, stating, pursuant to the decision of the Birac Serb autonomous region government, which regulates the moving out of the Muslim population from the territory of Birac Serb autonomous region, "I hereby order, one, set up a camp in Vlasenica and secure it in compliance with international regulations. Two, I forbid the passing of any arbitrary decision on the physical liquidation of prisoners." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, we've heard evidence during the course of this case that -- that's okay. Let me move on from that question. In any event, Mr. Krajisnik, these two documents reflect in one area Muslim men of military age being taken into camps for exchange, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why that was done, but I can remind you of a witness from Hadzici who was here and who said that all people, all civilians, had been taken -- had been placed under arrest by Muslims. So such people were exchanged too but that was not the policy and I didn't know about it. In one place, Serbs were placed under arrest and in another place, Hadzici, Muslims placed them under arrest. Of course, there were militarily able but that shouldn't have been done any way. I can't think of any other reason. All I know is that in Sekovici, Tuzla, and other places, Muslims, on the Muslim side, placed a lot of people under arrest and they spent the whole war in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We just looked at two documents arising from events in Eastern Bosnia. Perhaps we can look quickly at a couple of documents arising from events in Western Bosnia. So if I could ask you to turn to tab 262, that will need a number, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1243, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1243 is a communication from the chief of the public security station, Simo Drljaca to the ministry, Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of the Interior security services centre Banja Luka dated 31 May 1992. And in it, Mr. Drljaca indicates that "with a view to the speedy and effective establishment of peace on the territory of Prijedor municipality, and in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff, I hereby order the following. 1, the industrial compound of the Omarska mine strip mine shall serve as a provisional collection centre for persons captured in combat or detained on the grounds of the security services operational information." In item number 3 he states that a mixed group consisting of national, public, and military security investigators shall be responsible for the work with and categorisation of detainees. They shall organise themselves respecting the parity principle. Mirko Jesic, Ranko Mijic, and Lieutenant Colonel Majstorovic, shall be responsible for their work." Now, with respect to item 3, Mr. Krajisnik, it appears to me that the parity principle refers to the fact that persons from different arms of the Bosnian Serb MUP or military structure will be involved, including Mr. Jesic, Ranko Mijic, and then clearly an army officer, Lieutenant Colonel Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if we could also look at a document in connection with that, which is found at the next tab, tab 263.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a June 1, 1992 confidential report from the 1st Krajina Corps, from Colonel Milutin Vukelic from the 5th Corps command to the 1 KK Corps command and looking at the very bottom of page 1 in the English, and the first full paragraph on page 2 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, the report states, "The heaviest fighting has taken place in the area of Hambarine, Prijedor and Kozarac. Troops under the command of the Prijedor area cleared Hambarine and Kozarac, and completely destroyed one ZNG unit, black shirts, foreign mercenaries and legionnaires, the troops have arrested more than 2.000 Green Berets who are now in Omarska. 135 of them are in Stara Gradiska prison and about 5.000 in the village of Trnopolje." Mr. Krajisnik, these two documents, then, reflect the establishment of Omarska and other camps into which were placed Muslims who had been captured by or arrested by the army or by the Bosnian Serb MUP. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is written here, I think. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as these camps began to fill up with more people, new camps were also established, and if I could ask you to turn to tab 277.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is P872, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a strictly confidential communication from Major Svetozar Andric, commander of the Birac Brigade to the commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps saying on June 17th, at item number 2, "it is necessary to urgently resolve the issue of prisoner camps because in Vlasenica we currently have 640 prisoners. The safety situation in town is in danger because of this. And similarly if I could ask you quickly in connection with that to turn to tab 265, it's an earlier document but -- and perhaps I should have turned to it first. Your Honour, tab 265 is or contains P1065. A daily operations report from the commander of the East Bosnia Corps, Colonel Ilic, to the Main Staff of the Srpska -- of the VRS. And there, commander Ilic states at items 8 and 9, "We have around 560 prisoners in the region of Zvornik and around 800 in the region of Vlasenica. In item 9, "we ask to you carry out the command [as read] from previous days. The demand, excuse me, if I misstated it. The transcript says, "we ask to you to carry out the command." Item 9 says "demand." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, I believe we've heard previous evidence that the 560 prisoners in the region of Zvornik were persons held in the Karakaj technical school and around 800 in the region of Vlasenica refer to the Susica camp. Do you have any reason to dispute that information?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it just as you did, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we -- so we see the commander Ilic talking about the prisoners who were being held in areas of Eastern Bosnia and then we have seen the concern expressed by Major Andric on June 17th concerning the number of prisoners in Vlasenica. If we could turn then to tab 276.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which is P874, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P874 is an urgent and strictly confidential order from General Mladic to the Eastern Bosnia Corps Command, and to the commander personally. And if we look down that first full paragraph, to -- which is broken down into a number of separate sections, numerically, and the 4th sentence, there is an item 1, and then in describing the problems as follows, in the middle of the paragraph, there are four items enumerated. If we look at the third, about four lines up from the bottom of the page on page 1, and it's also page 1 in your version, Mr. Krajisnik, General Mladic states, "The brigade has close to 600 prisoners. You did not establish a camp for war prisoners at corps level." And then turning to page 2 of the English, and page 2 of the B/C/S, under the item number 2, and you'll find that, Mr. Krajisnik, at the -- you'll see there is a longish paragraph and then a break in the text and then another sentence, that's the sentence I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the English, Your Honours, it's the third indented -- indicated by a dash, organ under item 2, "the corps is to set up a camp of war prisoners pursuant to our order, confidential number 18/28-6, dated June 12th, 1992. The brigade is to be relieved of guarding prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And one more item in that regard, Mr. Krajisnik, if you can turn to tab 290. We may need another bundle for that, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will need an a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1244, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1244 is an order pursuant to the order by the army of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Main Staff, confidential number 18/28-6, dated 12 June 1992, regarding the accommodation, daily organisation for life and work of the persons arrested in combat or during their crimes against the people, and it states, in item number 1, establish camp for prisoners of war on a farm in the village of Batkovic for collection of arrested people. The camp shall operate under the name "farm." Item number 2 the commander of the East Bosnia Corps shall appoint the commander of the camp in his order. Mr. Krajisnik, looking at these documents, we can see in Eastern Bosnia a reflection of concern about the number of prisoners and the establishment of additional camps such as Batkovic at the corps level in response to that problem, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I am reading this just the way you are. I can read what you're reading too, but I'm not familiar with any of this. May I just add something? It has to do with what is -- what seems to be your intention. Mr. Mladic attended meetings with us only twice during the course of 1992. That is on the 9th of June and in August. If you think that he came coming to see us all the time, contact us, report to us, believe me all of that is wrong. You can have a look at all the meetings. Nobody informed us about this. Nobody informed me about this, at least, whether somebody else was informed, I don't know but there are two meetings only between Mr. Mladic and the members of the Presidency, meetings that I attended, too. So I don't know any of all of this and I can only confirm what you're reading out, if this is correct and I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, earlier we looked at both Eastern Bosnia, events in Eastern Bosnia and some events in Western Bosnia. If we can turn back to Western Bosnia at tab 266 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are really persistent. My hat is off to you. Please go ahead. 266.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 266, Your Honours is P11, P200 and P529 tab 306. This -- these are the -- or this document contains the conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most on 4 June 1992, including the following: "Number 1, Mirko Vrucinic, Nedjelko Rasula, and Colonel Nedjo Anicic shall be in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca," and it also contains a list of the categories, first category, politicians; second category, nationalist extremists; third category, people unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality. It continues, "in view of this have a talk with Colonel Stevilovic from the 1st Krajina Corps." So Mr. Krajisnik, this document reflects the existence of an operation of the Manjaca camp by June 4th, 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. But I can see here that it's there. I didn't know about Manjaca then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And also reflects, as we've seen in previous orders, directives, and documents, the process of categorisation for the prisoners, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what is written here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we turn to tab 277, P872 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I'm sorry, that would be tab 278?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because we had seen 277 earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, accordingly the exhibit number would be different. It would be P748. Tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the 36th session of the Petrovac municipality Crisis Staff held on 17 June 1992, and turning to an item under decisions, on page 4 of the English, and Mr. Krajisnik, page 00946833, that is page 2 of the B/C/S, it's the second-to-last of the decisions item on that page which states, "On the level of the 2nd Krajina Corps the prisoners from the Petrovac public security station are to be transferred to Prekaja or to Manjaca." And again, Mr. Krajisnik, it refers to the operation of the Manjaca camp at -- in June of 1992, where prisoners from various municipalities were sent after being captured or arrested?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is your question whether I knew about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the first question is that -- in -- that is an accurate reflection of those documents in so far as you know, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any of these things. A witness was here from Petrovac. He told you about this and he explained this whole situation to you and he told you that I was not in contact with them. Jovo Radojko. I didn't know about any of these things that you asked me about, so far, and no one contacted me in that regard. I didn't know about a single one of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, by late May and -- well, let me -- during the course of your examination-in-chief, I noted, on May 23rd, Mr. Stewart asked you about camps, and he confronted you with some of the testimony by ambassador Okun, about the establishment of camps in -- by June of 1992, and the -- what he called the lengthy and painful discussion among the humanitarian agencies with the Bosnian Serb leadership about what to do with the people because it's a terrible moral dilemma. You indicated-- this is about 5422 is where this passage starts, "I learned that here and I don't challenge that." So, by -- my question is, Mr. Krajisnik, by late May and certainly by June, the international community was concerned, deeply concerned, about the existence of camps in which Muslims and Croats were held, and about expulsions of Muslims, and that concern was made known to the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said to you that I was never involved in this, and that I wasn't even informed about it. I gave you documents here stating that Drljaca himself said that there are no camps in their area. At the end of July the Minister of the MUP is asking whether there are any camps in their area. If he didn't flow about it, how could I know? I knew about prisoners in general, that they were supposed to be exchanged, and but I don't know where they were, where the camps were, who established the camps, none of that, and that's what I said to Stewart too. Who opened Susica, Batkovici, Manjaca, I didn't know anything about that. I didn't know that these camps existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We are going to go through this but in connection with your assertion that at the end of July, the Minister of the MUP was asking Drljaca about camps and wasn't told about it, why don't we turn quickly to tab 297?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He asked Mr. Zupljanin and Zupljanin asked Drljaca. I provided that material here. That's what I have, and I don't even know whether that's accurate either. I gave it to you on that CD.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understood you to be asserting that in so far as you were aware, the MUP, either at the regional level or at the republic level was unaware of Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, at the end of July because Drljaca was denying that they existed.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is what I said. I did not know about a single camp and in order to prove that to you, that the Minister of the MUP could not even have informed me about this, I gave you the papers that I found here. I didn't have them then. Where he is receiving misinformation stating that there are no camps in Prijedor. Now, whether the minister knew or not, I don't know. But on the basis of the papers, I saw that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at other documents reflecting what the minister did or didn't know but for now I just want you to look at the document at tab 297 which will need a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1245, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1245, Your Honours is a dispatch dated 1 August 1992 from Simo Drljaca, the chief of the public security station, to the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to the Banja Luka security services centre, informing them that at a meeting held on July 24th, 1992, the War Presidency of the Prijedor municipal assembly adopted a decision, number provided, pursuant to which the reserve police force presently employed should be greatly reduced and the security for the Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska reception centres provided by the army. So it would seem, Mr. Krajisnik, that Mr. Drljaca, far from keeping the existence of Keraterm, Trnopolje and Omarska a secret, was communicating with the Ministry of the Interior, at both republic and regional levels about its existence and -- about their existence and operation.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you couldn't read all of this because it's in Cyrillic but it says we do not have the possibility to send it. That's what is added on to the original. He probably didn't manage to send it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll see other communications about the camps in western Bosnia but it is clear that he --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he sent it. I'm just reading out what's written here. And I know what I saw. The decision, I mean. I mean, I don't know whether he reported about this. Maybe he did. But the minister would not send him this question, asking him to brief him about whether there are any camps; there are not. I mean, that is a bit strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, from the document itself, there may exist some doubt on whether it was sent due to the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would say to Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour, there is no doubt however that Mr. Drljaca has any intent on keeping it a secret and there is no doubt from the document that he understands that all of the intended recipients know about the existence of these camp, isn't that right? Whether this particular document reached them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sat here and listened to the last 15 minutes. Mr. Krajisnik is being asked question after question about documents he really can't answer. He -- and that last question was a culmination of that line of cross-examination and was no more than a veiled comment wrapped up in a question. My learned friend in fact gave the game away by saying, "and I would say to Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour." That really shows where this cross-examination is going. It's comment, not proper cross-examination. The witness can't answer most of these questions in reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Josse, there is a problem. One could not exclude for the possibility that the witness could answer such questions or comment on the material, for example by saying in the 1st of August 1992, Mr. Drljaca was having a party in Hannover rather than -- so I do agree with you that the matter could be dealt with in one general question, which -- of which we have heard the answer several times, that is that Mr. Krajisnik didn't know anything about the existence of camps, the establishment of camps, adding camps to existing camps, he was not involved and he was not informed about it. At the same time, if Mr. Tieger would not put at least to the witness these documents, then he would also deprive the witness from pointing at matters he does know, which cast a certain light on these documents. So therefore, Mr. Tieger, perhaps when you summarise them and say doesn't this reflect, et cetera, et cetera. If Mr. Krajisnik is not aware of the documents, we can read what the documents say and of course we can read the documents in context with the other documents. So to some extent I do agree that if I say well, it's uncertain whether it was sent or not that you comment on it. Of course, it could have been put in a question form as well, to say the fact that it has not been sent, does that mean in your view that Mr. Drljaca, by drafting or at least formulating this dispatch, whether that could in any way be -- or whether the witness has any reason to understand this to be anything else than what it obviously does, that is to teach other people about what happened. To some extent I agree with you, to some extent I also do not because at a later stage, the Prosecution might be blamed for not having put it to the witness. But perhaps with a little bit less comment it would do well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Briefly with respect, I agree and accept what Your Honour has just said and as the Court is well aware, the Defence are anxious that as many documents as possible are put to Mr. Krajisnik during the course of his examination regardless who -- of who is asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So that extent I endorse what Your Honour has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And of course there was some comments on my side as well that we should not use -- we should not use the document to -- well, to put things in it which everyone who reads the documents can read and so interpretation of the documents, if Mr. Krajisnik can't give it, the Chamber is perfectly able to read it and also deduce from your questions what are the most relevant portions and what you're mainly interested to hear comments on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just add something. The documents that I presented bear this same date, and he says that there are no camps there. The month was August. You have it there. Those were the documents that I received. But I didn't know of them before either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So neither the confirming nor the denying report, your testimony is, Mr. Krajisnik, is that you were aware of them at the time. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I beg your pardon. I believe that Trnopolje, Keraterm, and Omarska existed. Now I know. But I didn't know at the time. That's the only thing that I'm saying. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please turn to tab 258, Mr. Krajisnik. That is P583, tab 52. P583, tab 52 is a letter dated May 24th, 1992, from the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, Branko Djeric, to James Baker?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That 258? Sorry, it says 253, and I found 258.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, 258 is the correct tab.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I indicated that's a letter drafted May 24th, 1992, from Prime Minister Djeric to James Baker, the Secretary of state of the United States, and he begins by stating, "We have just received the most disturbing news about decisions of the ministerial conference of NATO in Lisbon, Portugal, suggesting the use of force against Serbian population in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then he goes on to discuss the issues that have prompted the suggestions that force might be employed against Serbs. In the last paragraph of the English, and also the last paragraph of the B/C/S, on the first page, Your Honours, and Mr. Krajisnik, Prime Minister Djeric states, "You can rest assured that Serbian side is holding no hostages, operating no concentration camps, and is not killing unarmed civilians in Bosnia. The reports alleging such crimes, appearing in the US press and elsewhere are not based on facts. Mr. Krajisnik, this document reflects the awareness of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including but not limited to Dr. Djeric, about the allegations by the international community that the Bosnian Serbs were rounding people up, putting them in camps, and the concern by the Bosnian Serbs that the international community might intervene as a result.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this letter either. But the Prime Minister wrote this letter on the basis of somethings that were written in the press of the United States and he is denying that there are camps and that there are killings. That's probably his knowledge. Mr. Djeric certainly knew this as far as I know him. That is to say, his knowledge was that there were no concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And no one brought to your attention, Mr. Krajisnik, the "most disturbing news," that the international community was contemplating the use of force against Serbs because of allegations of Bosnian Serb crimes against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I know that there was this threat by NATO but I don't remember the time. Certainly there was a threat all the time, because we were illegal and the Muslim side was the legal authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for some parties. And there was always something that was brought up. I also brought you documents about this propaganda that was carried out, that there was intentional propaganda coming from a centre, at that time, in that period, you can look it up in the documents that I provided. There is a video clip too. At that time, I didn't know about that. But I'm telling you, other people were involved in these matters and they responded appropriately. I never wrote this letter. I didn't read this press after all, but I heard a lot of information and misinformation, a lot. We were attacked all the time. We were being blamed all the time. We, the Serbs. That is true. I understand Mr. Djeric's letter to mean that he is justifying himself, saying that he was not aware of any such thing at all. That is the way I understand his letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how long the Court wishes to go but I wouldn't be loath to begin a question with 30 seconds remaining before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll have a break first --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that Mr. Krajisnik is going to read tab 191. The Defence were going to ask to go and see Mr. Krajisnik about matters unrelated to his evidence. I mentioned it earlier to my learned friends. Mr. Stewart should be in the building by now and is going to accompany me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're asking for more time for the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not, Your Honour. Mr. Krajisnik could read 191, overnight, frankly and make any comment about it tomorrow morning. That's what I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, and my suggestion would be, if -- it appeared to me Mr. Krajisnik was going to take the break to read the document, maybe the visit by Mr. Josse and Mr. Stewart could be delayed until after court so we don't lose any additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be a problem in transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know. I'd prefer Mr. Krajisnik to read 191 now so that we do not forget about it and tomorrow have to refresh our memories about what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I take it that it would not take more -- from what I saw, most of the issues in that interview are not directly related to the portion put to Mr. Krajisnik. So Mr. Krajisnik, if you would start reading the last -- well, the last one or two issues and then start having a glance at the other issues, because there are headings always, what it is about, and see whether you can fit this in and have a short meeting with Mr. Stewart and Mr. Josse as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, what was it? What was the number? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 191, Your Honour. I'll double check.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President? I brought you some documents today. Namely when Prevlaka was handed over. That was what was in dispute yesterday. I brought a document about where the Serbs were supposed to have access to the sea. That was a subject of the debate here yesterday. That's Owen's book which also exists in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore I gave it to the parties to see whether Defence counsel and Prosecution would consider it useful to bring it to our attention. If they do not revisit the matter, we might have a look at it and see whether we are interested in it. But to be quite fair to the parties, the issue of the access of the sea was not considered such as we discussed yesterday, that we would spend much more time on that because it seems that the same is to some extent true for Sarajevo as well, is among the strategic goals are the ones who were -- are less linked to what is the core of this case. Sarajevo, of course, is different from the access to the sea but especially the access to the sea was not something that we are seeking much more information about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zimmermann's statement, I brought it here in its entirety. It's very important because it's different from what the mere excerpt shows and I also brought a video of Mr. Zimmermann because that was the Prosecutor's argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm just urging the Court, Your Honour, not to take up time with a recital of what's been provided us here on paper. If we'd all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the procedure, that respect is clear, and the Court, of course, takes the [indiscernible] point, Mr. Krajisnik, that if there is anything in that material which is not yet in evidence and what really could assist in your Defence, that they will certainly not overlook it. At the same time, the Chamber does not exclude for the possibility that it will ask for material, as we did before. We will have a break until five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, shortly before the break, we had looked at Prime Minister Djeric's letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am very sorry. Is the Chamber not going to ask Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I had forgotten that. I apologise. Mr. Krajisnik, did you have an opportunity to read 19 -- tab number 191?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have read it, glanced through it either, but I have something to say in connection with that document briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you do that, briefly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. That is an interview related to the blockade imposed by Serbia on Republika Srpska, and the words that I have uttered there are inappropriate and really, it's almost as if it wasn't me who said them. But I can't deny them now. Even if I had uttered them in anger, that's not very smart, because for as long as my memory serves me, I never advocated such a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One housekeeping matter. Yesterday the Court asked for still images of the map video. We have those here and can provide them to the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I think there is no objection that we do not give any specific number to it. It's just an aid to what we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And could I look at one as well, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could have Your Honour's for a moment. Perhaps I could have Judge Hanoteau's just for a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine if the Prosecution -- if they have a copy for me later that's fine. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, as I indicated before, shortly before we recessed, we had looked at Prime Minister Djeric's letter of May 24th 1992, concerning allegations by and concerns of the international community. I would now like to turn to some documents --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just remind you -- remind me, which tab is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm about to do so. I'm not going to return to that document. We are going to look at some events that followed.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if we could turn to tab 268?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P64, P65, tab 157, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The minutes of the 5th session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of BH on 10 June 1992, present, Dr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, Dr. Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Djeric. As we see, at the very beginning of the document, after the attendees are listed, at the beginning of the session, the Presidency reviewed information received during the night on the situation at the front, and reports of the international public. Mr. Krajisnik, that's a reflection of the continuing concern about what was being reported and alleged about, among other things, Bosnian Serb activities during the war, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It's simply -- I told you, somebody would come with certain information and inform us about what was happening in a particular area. It could be a representative of the government or I don't know who, somebody who was informed, but it was -- it was more like a piece of information being shared, but you're right, we were interested in what was going on, whether we had lost a municipality somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the reference to reports of the international public, in contrast to the information received about the situation at the front, is a reflection of the continuing interest in what the international community was saying and alleging and perceiving?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. Koljevic or I don't know who else would brief us about what he knew, what he may have seen on television or heard, or had found out in his contacts with the international community, with regard to allegations and I don't know what else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before we continue, there is a -- the "international public" is the translation of the words and then it says, with a question mark, foreign press. I would like to know from the interpreters whether this is another way of translating or whether it is a kind of interpretation of what may have been meant with it although not reflected by the words itself. Could the interpreters -- you have both the B/C/S and the English translation? Yes. Could you enlighten us as to what the question mark exactly should mean to us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The translation given here, international public, or reports of the international public, is correct, and it's literal and it does probably refer to foreign press and media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- so the words public is not publications or something like that but just to give it some sense with a question mark, you have suggested that it might have to be understood in this way. Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking at the very bottom of the page, in English, and page 2 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, immediately below the listing of the persons appointed commissioners, the minutes indicate that at the session, the Presidency issued the following assignments, including, as we turn to the second page of the English, the third entry, to Dr. Djeric, and the second assignment, which Dr. Djeric received was, for the government to report on detainees with proposal of measures. Mr. Krajisnik, was that a response to the information received about the situation at the front, the reports of the international public or foreign press, or some other information?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this refers to but it's obvious that this body is not informed and requires information from Mr. Djeric on any issue at all. I know there were prisons, but I don't know what the conditions in those prisons were, prisons opened by the assembly, the government, but there were other prisons apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So whatever the source of the information prompting that assignment, the Presidency was interested in receiving a report on detainees along with proposals of measures to be taken in connection with that issue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And that was mentioned on many occasions later, as well. But if you would like to move on from this record, these minutes, I would like an opportunity to say something briefly before you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to be moving to another document from the same date so, if --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I would just like to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, sorry, if it's on the same subject we are addressing right now. The subject, the issue of detainees and --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it concerns these minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The question was mainly about the issue raised during this meeting about detainees and the international -- reports from international --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not about prisoners, let's move on. I wanted to mention Aleksa Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn next, then, to tab 270 which is P64, P65, tab 156, and P583, tab 20. Now, these are the minutes from the 25th government session held on the same date, chaired by Mr. Djeric, and if we turn to page 3 of the English and page 2 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, under item 7, which appears at the bottom of page 2 of the English and then it states at the top of page 3, current issues, so in the discussion of current issues we see that the following conclusions were made. That the Ministry of Justice should make a report about prisoners. This report should pay special attention on treatment of civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera. The report would be considered by the government after which it would be submitted to the Presidency of the republic. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, that was Mr. Djeric's immediate response to the assignment he had received at the session of the Presidency the same day, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be the other way around, that he said what he would do and it was recorded that way, but on the same day, I don't know which session came first. It could be, you're really right, this consultative meeting could have been in the morning and this session later. Yes, you are right. He was given that task and he entrusted it to the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to tab 272, and that is P64A, P583, tab 23, these are the minutes from the 28th government meeting held on June 15th, five days after the government meeting we have just looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarify case on the previous matter before you continue, Mr. Tieger? The -- in item 7 it says that the Minister of Justice should make a report about prisoners, and then it continues, this report should pay special attention on treatment of civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera. It gives the impression that civilian population is an issue when you're talking about prisoners. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you saying that to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm just telling you what the language I would say suggests by putting civilian population in an item which deals with prisoners. It doesn't say civilian criminals or something like that. It doesn't say -- it says treatment of civilian population as being a part of a report on prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just need to find this, current issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one. Tab 270.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand this as follows, Your Honour: The Ministry of Justice should prepare a brief about detained persons, detainees, in which, meaning in which brief, special attention should be paid to the issue of treatment of civilian population. Then prisoners of war. Then accommodation, food and such like. He refers to a brief where all this should be covered. It could be that the prisoners are in prison but he could also be speaking about the treatment of civilian population. I don't know which is true, but civilian population is mentioned here, but it says this brief should cover or pay separately or pay special attention to the treatment of civilian population. The best thing to do would be to take that report that they made and see what they did, from that we will see how they performed this task. I mean, the commission who received that task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking you this question because it -- at least this language suggests, and of course we -- the Chamber will have to decide on whether that is a suggestion we would follow, that when you're writing about prisoners, that this would include civilian population and therefore to be understood as civilian population in prisons, which -- and I'm just putting it to you so that you have a fair opportunity to comment to it -- which suggests also that in the documents on what was -- that the document -- this document, which tells us whether at least those present and that's of course not everyone but that at least it was understood that reports on prisoners would have to do something with civilian population, which might be easily understood as civilian population in prisons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can understand it in different ways. I'm just telling you I don't know what this is but I'm trying to explain that if they are sending it to a commission, they don't know what is there in prisons, whether there are civilians, whether there are others. It's the report that shows what the commission had found. So it's best to take the report and see if there are any civilians. I'm not saying that your suggestion is wrong. I am just saying I don't know. I'm not denying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I had asked you to turn to tab 272, the government session held five days later, and in particular, if we could turn to agenda item 10, on page 4 of the English, and page 01245374 at the very top of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, and page 10 appears in approximately the middle of page 4 of the English, Your Honours, which states, "The government has considered the proposed report. It has been concluded that the issue of prisoners exchange is extremely important, complex and delicate, and that if sufficient attention is not paid to it, it can cause a number of negative consequences for the whole republic. It has been agreed that a working group consisting of Professor Branko Djeric, Milan Trbojevic, Dr. Dragan Kalinic, Mico Stanisic, Bogdan Subotic and Momcilo Mandic should consider all the aspects of the prisoner exchange problem and that they should propose systematic and other solutions taking into account our and international regulations. It is obvious that solving this problem is urgent and that the regulations and concrete measures for solving of this issue should be proposed as soon as possible." So, Mr. Krajisnik, it appears that five days later the government received the report related to prisoners, and having received that report, it concluded that if it wasn't attended to, it could cause a number of negative consequences, indeed, that were extremely important, for the whole republic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked up the agenda, and this is a report by Mr. Colovic. Look at the agenda and you will see. That's what was discussed. It says, "Brief on the improvement of the central commission for exchange."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- well, Mr. Krajisnik, the central commission for exchange was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice, correct? We've seen that in earlier evidence.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just now you saw the report of Mr. Colovic. That was on the agenda. We discussed a moment ago that commission, and it was said that measures should be taken to improve. That's the material we read before the break. It says, "central commission for the exchange of prisoners." It's on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's just try to see what's on the agenda and what's not. First of all, Mr. Colovic is not present at the session on June 15th, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was present, but that brief was there. It's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice was tasked on June 15th to make a report about prisoners. That we agree on. We've just also agreed that the commission for exchange was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice, and you previously indicated, in looking at those orders, and documents we looked at this morning, that the commission for exchange had responsibility for prisoners of war and detainees, which included both prisoners of war and civilians, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't comment on it at all. Please, just read the agenda, and look at the heading that refers to the document of Rajko Colovic. The same one as the one on the agenda, where he warns that many things have to be taken care of, regulated, et cetera. Whether he was actually at the session, I don't know, but they could not have prepared that report in five days. They made it later. I mean the report about prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Colovic order of June 6th indicates, among other things, that all information about prisoners is to be submitted to the commission for exchange and that no one is to be released without prior order of the commission for exchange. You can look at that if you want or you can take my word for it. But if that's the case, then doesn't it make sense, Mr. Krajisnik, that when the Ministry of Justice was tasked to make a report about prisoners, they would consult with or give the task to the commission for exchange?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, are you denying that this is the agenda? Do you continue to insist on your theory? I am trying to tell you for the third time now that this is the agenda. How to improve the work of the central commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I don't think that there is any disagreement that Mr. Tieger think that is when you're referring -- yes, but you're making a gesture as if all questions have been resolved by saying this is the agenda. I'm afraid that it's more complex, and Mr. Tieger does not only refer to the agenda but also refers to what he reads elsewhere. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to tab 274, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I admitted when I make a mistake and I always say what is correct but I think that it is impermissible for us to move the wrong way all the time, but okay, I'll go ahead. What was it that you said? 274?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me -- okay. Your Honour, I would like to move quickly through this but perhaps one more question would be appropriate. I had asked you a question, Mr. Krajisnik, about the Ministry of Justice, the commission for exchange, and their relationship in connection with the tasking of the Ministry of Justice to produce a report about what was happening with prisoners, both civilian and prisoners of war. So my question is: Is it -- is there no connection between a report by the commission for exchange, if indeed that -- a report about improving the work of the central commission for the exchange of prisoners of war, detained persons, et cetera, and the interest in -- by the government and the interest by the Presidency in finding out what was happening to prisoners of war and civilian detainees? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instead of me getting angry, you're getting angry. I assure you that these are two different questions, different questions. The Presidency instructed the government to give a report on the detainees. That is one thing. And they looked at the subject matter that had to do with detainees. And they said that the work of the central commission had to be improved. The government submitted reports on prisoners. There are three reports here, Eastern Bosnia, Eastern Herzegovina, Western Bosnia and you've got all the reports here based on those instructions. This was not a report on detainees, on prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is no. The question was whether there is no connection and then your answer is there is no connection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you explained why you take -- why you gave that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll come to those reports that you just mentioned Mr. Krajisnik, but perhaps it's useful to admit to the Judges right now that those reports were commissioned in and not received until -- they were commissioned in August of 1992, after the international community gained access to Omarska, and they were received in August of 1992 and October of 1992. They don't have any relationship to this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should say what it is you want and I'll explain to it to you very nicely and I'm telling you that this is not correct. When the Presidency was informed, they immediately asked the government to submit a report. And they reacted to all the reports they received.
