Not only if the international community said that but even if a single individual had said that. I'm so sorry but I cannot confirm your thesis. After all I'm not familiar with it but I'm telling you that these two things do not mix.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please turn to tab 274. Tab 274 is P65, tab 163.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said to 74?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to look at this very quickly and then turn to 275. Tab 274 contains the minutes of the 7th session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 16th of June 1992, and again we see present, Dr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, Dr. Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Dr. Djeric. Item number 1 is, at the session the Presidency was briefed on the situation in the field and took a position regarding daily activities. So that happened the date after the receipt by the government and its formation of a commission of its highest-ranking members concerning the issue of prisoners. Did the discussion on the situation in the field on the 16th concern, among other things, the problem of prisoners exchange that was so important, complex and delicate that it triggered the establishment of a commission consisting of the government's highest-ranking members?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My lawyer cautioned me that I should not get angry at the Prosecutor because you're just doing your job. So I will not do that. This has nothing to do with prisoners. And a commission has to be set up to see what the situation is regarding prisoners, and the government actually did that. And they got a report. You don't get reports over the telephone. I apologise to the Prosecutor. He's doing his job. This has nothing to do with anything. Everybody was receiving some kind of information from the field but this is agency information or whatever. I don't know how to call it. We were interested in who, what, where, how.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just when did Dr. Djeric get back to the Presidency concerning the requested and tasked report on detainees with proposals -- with proposal of measures?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not phrased properly. Perhaps the interpretation is not good. I'm sorry. Could you please rephrase your question or could you, rather, put it again so that I'd see what is going on? It's as if Djeric had asked for something. What is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On June 10th, the president tasked Dr. Djeric to obtain a report on detainees with proposals of measures. On June 15th, he received a report indicating a problem so -- with regard to prisoners, so delicate and important that it jeopardised the republic. You're telling me that on June 16th, when Dr. Djeric was at the meeting of the Presidency, he didn't say anything about the prisoner problem. So I'm asking you just when did he get back to you in response to that assignment?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report on prisoners did not come in on the 15th of June. No. Much later. That's a report on the problems of the central commission. Please, that's the way it is. For sure. I don't know what's written in English, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please turn to tab 275, which is P65, P583, tab 24. These are the minutes from the 30th session of the Serb Republic of BH government held on 17 June 1992 chaired by Dr. Djeric. And, Your Honours, if you can turn to agenda item 10, which begins at the bottom of page 5 but actually appears on page 6?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, that's at page 5 of your version.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. That's at -- okay. That is something I wanted to bring your attention to but not at this moment. Please turn to the very last item, page 7 of the English and page 6 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it. Now, that's what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The government has concluded that all measures be taken promptly for a more efficient work of the republic commission for the exchange of prisoners. With regard to this fact it is necessary to secure the accommodation and other conditions according to a previous decision of the government, the Ministry of Justice is in charge."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I was telling you. The commission and the conditions for supporting their work. See? The commissions are moving out in the field to see what the situation was like in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the complex and sensitive and important problem referred to in the government session of 15 June was the same problem that you had referred to in your testimony in chief, that is that prisoners and detainees were not being exchanged fast enough with the result that many were remaining in prison and were, as you put it, in your testimony, easy prey for many irresponsible people in terms of abuse, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my comment. The comment that I got subsequently. But I knew that international humanitarian organisations were acting as intermediaries in order to reach an agreement on an exchange of all for all. It's a problem if you have prisoners. Of course. And another thing, Mr. Prosecutor, there are also dead bodies of ours on their territory. That's a problem. When you have prisoners, you want to have an exchange all for all. You don't know how many there are any way. And later on there were exchanges of lists, too. Everything. But that was done by the commission separately. Here, well, I establish this because anybody can read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, as the success of the Bosnian Serb military forces increased, so did the problem of prisoners and detainees mount and increase as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war, we wanted to exchange prisoners, all for all. We believed that prisoners should be exchanged. One of our prisoners should be released even for ten of theirs. They always wanted to have provisional solutions, partial solutions, but throughout the war, we wanted prisoners to be released. And that, response to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I just was about to say that it is not a response to the question of Mr. Tieger. Mr. Tieger said, once the success of the military forces increased, whether the problem of the prisoners increased as well? Not asking what the problems were in resolving that problem but whether the problem of prisoners increased together with the success of the military forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It did not increase, Mr. President. It was always the same. Regardless of whether you had one or ten. It was always the same. It was big.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn quickly to the 17th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly? I just want to look quickly at two portions. This was the session held on July 24th to 26th, latter part of July 1992 and just quickly Mr. Krajisnik, turning to page 14 of the English and page 11 of your version, and Your Honour without line numbering it's a little difficult to identify that portion but it's just slightly below the precise middle of the page on page 14. Where Dr. Karadzic states, "Today we control all of our territories and perhaps also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the minus one situation there, Mr. Tieger? Please proceed. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Today we control all of ore territories and perhaps also some territories that will be given to other national communities once a deal is reached." And then I'd also like you to turn, Mr. Krajisnik, to page --.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, 32 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, that's at page 31 of your version, and I suspect, given the minus one problem, probably page 31 of the English for the Court as well. It's the final portion of Mr. Milanovic's remarks. And probably about 20 lines up from the bottom, where he states, "We have a huge problem with captured people of other nationalities. We have hundreds and thousands of these prisoners." Now, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, did you find that section?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we found it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a reflection of two things, Mr. Krajisnik, isn't it? The continuing military success of the Bosnian Serb forces and the ongoing problem, indeed, as Mr. Milanovic said, huge problem of captured people of other nationalities, both of which were brought to the attention of the assembly in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And at the London Conference we agreed on an exchange, all for all. It was immediately after this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock, which tells me that we have to finish for the day. Mr. Tieger, the Chamber told the Prosecution that they should head for finishing by tomorrow. At the same time, we have to consider, since we lost quite sometime today, whether it would be fair to just add one thing and we'll also further look at the statistics as we did for the Defence, to see whether the Judges have taken more time than usual. I mean, we are thinking in terms of days, but today we lost half a day, just as in the beginning with the Defence. Also the Chamber has been a bit more strict and not -- I think we don't have the full 60 per cent. So therefore, we will consider whether some, and I'm hesitant to say, some additional time will be granted in compensation for that, just as we did compensate for a few matters for the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.
